newsitem.title: USA: NYS Pataki's plan seen ending rent rules in 8 yrs.
newsitem.headline: NYS Pataki's plan seen ending rent rules in 8 yrs.

text.p: New York State Gov George Pataki declined to say how long it would take for rent rules to end under the new plan he unveiled Monday, but a tenant advocate predicted it would kill the system in eight years.
"We think the governor's plan would result in the complete phase-out of regulations, probably about eight years," said McKee, rent law campaign manager, for the Tenants & Neighbors Coalition.
McKee spoke to reporters after the Republican governor unveiled his new plan. The coalition calls itself the largest tenant advocacy group in the state.
Pataki, who said he stepped into the fray because the Assembly and Senate were not making progress in resolving the issue, which has held up the state's budget, now six weeks late.
The Republican governor focused on his program's open-ended nature, which avoids the two- or perhaps four-year limit proposed by Senate Majority Leader, Joseph Bruno, R-Troy.
"We have no arbitrary date at which rent control would end," Pataki told reporters at a midtown news conference.
But Pataki's plan includes vacancy decontrol, which means that apartments would return to the free-market once tenants voluntarily moved or died, if near relatives did not want to them.
New civil and criminal penalities were proposed for landlords to prevent them from driving tenants out of their apartments.

The amount of income tenants would have to earn for each of two years would fall to $175,000 from $250,000, but regardless of their income, the elderly--those 62 years old or older--and the disabled would keep their protections.
Tenant advocates and the Assembly Speaker, Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, oppose vacancy decontrol, saying it failed when it was tried from 1971 to 1974, and then repealed.

In the first two-and-a-half years of the experiment with vacancy decontrol, rents in apartments that were returned to the free-market system shot up 52 percent in New York City, 47 percent in Nassau County and 45 percent in Westchester County, the Coalition said. It added 133,000 apartments per year wre decontrolled in that program.

Pataki's director of communications, Zenia Mucha, when asked by reporters after the governor's news conference how long it would take for the present system to end under the new plan, replied: "It depends." She explained that if three generations of a family lived in a regulated apartment that that is how long it would take.

The vast majority of the state's approximately 1.1 million rent-regulated apartments are in New York City, and the Speaker, who represents a Manhattan district, blasted the governor's new plan as "nothing new."

He said he wanted a new package that would address both landlords' and tenants' concerns, which would increase housing construction. "Last week I said to you why don't we just build affordable housing and eliminate rent control and rent stabilization by reaching the vacancy rate. A very practical way to have an orderly market in housing. By the nature of the laws that's the way to do it," he told reporters in Albany.

The Senate Majority Leader attacked Silver for wanting to link property tax relief to getting rent rules extended, adding he would not agree to extend the present rules, which expire on June 15, but was open to ending the rules more gradually.

"I originally proposed a phase-out over two years, with protections for the elderly, poor and disabled. I am open to a longer period of time as long as controls are eventually lifted," he said, in prepared remarks.

Pataki, who told reporters he would not project how long the present system of rent regulations would remain under his plan, did not elaborate when asked whether he was preparing a long-term plan to relieve the housing crisis. "We're looking at all elements."
Asked whether his plan would polarize neighborhoods, a concern raised by Silver, who says it would drive the middle-class out of New York, the governor reiterated his program was fair and balanced.
